figures.title: Greedy decoding and the degeneration loop
figures.caption: Greedy decoding takes the argmax, appends it, and runs the model again. When the context ends in "the the", the scores put "the" above "cat" and "dog"; taking "the" makes the context "the the the", an even stronger match for the repeated pattern, so "the" rises again. Each step is locally correct and the sequence still loops. The mechanism is self-reinforcement through the KV cache, not a decoding bug.
figures.alt: Four lanes across five steps. The context lane starts at the the, scores the next token, picks the argmax, appends it, and repeats. The scores lane shows the on top, then the gap widening after the append. The choice lane shows the selected three times. The explanation lane notes that the pattern was seen in training, becomes a stronger match, and is self-reinforcing.

data.note: Holtzman et al. documented this in 2019: maximising likelihood step by step produces text that loops, drifts and contradicts itself. The previous token's key and value sit in the cache; if attention puts weight on them and the context supplies no stronger signal, the same direction reaches the head again.

steps.label: The context ends in the the.
Scores put the above cat and dog because the pattern appeared in training.
Appending it makes the the the, a stronger match for the same pattern.
The score for the rises again; the loop is closed.

figures.title: Temperature sets the shape; the cut keeps a set
figures.caption: Temperature rescales logits before the cut; truncation then renormalises. On logits 4.0, 2.0 and 1.0 the T = 1 probabilities are 0.844, 0.114 and 0.042. T = 0.5 sharpens to 0.980 / 0.018 / 0.002; T = 2 flattens to 0.628 / 0.231 / 0.140. Top-k with k = 2 keeps mass 0.958 and renormalises to 0.881 / 0.119; top-p = 0.9 keeps the same two; min-p = 0.1 cuts at 0.0844 and keeps the same two.
figures.alt: Four lanes across six steps. The first three steps are the probability of tokens A, B and C at T = 1, T = 0.5 and T = 2. A reads 0.844, 0.980, 0.628; B reads 0.114, 0.018, 0.231; C reads 0.042, 0.002, 0.140. The last three steps apply top-k, top-p and min-p cuts: A and B survive at 0.881 and 0.119, C is cut, and the kept mass stays 0.958.

data.note: The three cuts coincide here because B clears both the cumulative target and the floor. They diverge elsewhere: ten tokens at 0.1 each are kept nine by top-p = 0.9 but five by top-k = 5; one token at 0.95 with the rest thin is kept alone by top-p but fifty by top-k = 50. Top-p admits a variable count that follows the shape; top-k fixes the count; min-p sets the floor at min_p × p_max = 0.1 × 0.844 = 0.0844.

steps.label: Sort descending and keep the top k = 2: mass 0.958.
Add probabilities until the running total reaches 0.9: the same two.
Drop everything below 0.0844, then renormalise: 0.881 and 0.119.

sources.note: Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (2019): greedy degeneration and nucleus (top-p) sampling.
Fan, Lewis and Dauphin, Hierarchical Neural Story Generation (2018): top-k sampling.
Nguyen et al., Min-p sampling (2024): a floor relative to the maximum probability.
Keskar et al., CTRL (2019): the repetition penalty that divides positive logits and multiplies negative ones.
